network.overall_strategy: This precursor-resolved network contains 10 distinct reaction-node sequences: four Strecker processing variants, two aldehyde-derived hydantoin variants, one ketoacid-derived hydantoin hypothesis, and three experimentally tested metal-catalyzed reductive-amination variants. They are not 10 independent mechanisms or 10 demonstrated de novo geochemical syntheses. Isobutyraldehyde and alpha-ketoisovaleric acid are explicitly supplied starting materials because the provided literature does not establish their production from simpler feedstocks under compatible conditions. The strongest directly demonstrated conversions are the three Kaur et al. catalyst variants; valine-specific hydantoin chemistry and alternative Strecker processing conditions remain hypotheses. Cyanohydrin-first paths represent an alternative precursor-capture sequence, not a claim of a separate elementary amination mechanism. Unresolved acetone/cyanide, thermal formaldehyde, shock, and radiolytic product networks are excluded rather than assigned invented coproduct balances. All represented net reactions conserve atoms; inferred coefficients do not represent experimental yields. Neutral parent formulas describe aqueous acid-base components, with protonation and counterions suppressed. All settings are anoxic. Surface reactions require sheltered water or pore residence despite strong incident UV. Biochemical denotes abiotic concentrated solutions or mineral interfaces, not enzymes. Branches are alternative reactors, not a single compatible mixture: cyanide must not enter the metal-hydrogenation reactors because it can poison their catalysts. Competing hydroxy-acid formation is represented separately and is not counted as a productive pathway. No stereoselection is established; the target has unspecified stereochemistry and racemic formation is expected. environment_formed records a representative setting, not an exclusive one.

reactions.name: Reversible formation of the isobutyraldehyde aldimine

conditions.other: Anoxic sheltered pool or pore water; proposed pH 8.5-9.5 with excess total ammonia. Maintain a liquid phase and limit aldehyde and ammonia volatilization. The imine is a transient equilibrium species, not an assumed isolable reservoir.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia adds to the aldehyde, giving a carbinolamine that reversibly eliminates water to form an aldimine. Subsequent cyanide capture can pull the equilibrium forward.
reactions.reasoning: Miller (1957) supports aldehyde-ammonia-aminonitrile chemistry as the basis of discharge amino-acid synthesis, and Ring et al. (1972) directly identified valine in discharge products. The proposed operating window is not a measured valine-specific optimum. Water disfavors imine accumulation, so capture must compete with hydrolysis. The branched aldehyde is supplied explicitly; these papers do not establish its environmental production rate or concentration.

reactions.name: Cyanide capture of the aldimine

conditions.other: Anoxic aqueous phase at proposed pH 8.5-9.5, allowing both ammonia and cyanide nucleophilicity. HCN denotes the total cyanide component after acid-base equilibration. Avoid strongly acidic processing until aminonitrile capture is complete.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide attacks the imine or iminium carbon and proton transfer gives 2-amino-3-methylbutanenitrile. Cyanide supplies the future carboxyl carbon.
reactions.reasoning: This is the established Strecker reaction class described by Miller (1957), consistent with the direct valine identification of Ring et al. (1972). The carbon skeleton is explicitly accounted for: the aldehyde contributes four carbons and cyanide contributes one. No mineral catalyst is justified by the supplied experiments. Valine-specific capture rates and competing cyanide-polymerization losses remain unquantified.

reactions.name: Alternative cyanohydrin-first capture of isobutyraldehyde

conditions.other: Anoxic, initially ammonia-poor water containing aldehyde and cyanide; proposed pH 8-9. Cyanohydrin formation is reversible. Sheltered residence reduces photochemical exposure, but environmental retention has not been quantified.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to the aldehyde carbonyl and protonation gives its cyanohydrin.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative network extension at the valine-specific environmental level. Carbonyl cyanohydrin formation is established chemistry, but the supplied Miller (1957) and Ring et al. (1972) findings do not validate a discrete isobutyraldehyde-cyanohydrin reservoir. This branch tests whether cyanide capture before ammonia enrichment changes precursor retention. It is not counted as a separately demonstrated prebiotic valine mechanism.

reactions.name: Net conversion of the cyanohydrin pool to valine aminonitrile

conditions.other: Ammonia enrichment of the cyanohydrin-containing water; proposed pH 8.5-9.5. Maintain exchange among cyanohydrin, aldehyde, imine and dissolved cyanide. Neither a conversion time nor a valine-specific yield is established.

reactions.mechanism: Net cyanohydrin-to-aminonitrile conversion through reversible carbonyl/cyanohydrin and carbonyl/imine equilibria followed by cyanide trapping. Direct displacement of hydroxide by ammonia is not asserted.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative valine-specific processing variant of the Strecker chemistry supported generally by Miller (1957). The net transformation is balanced, but the supplied literature does not demonstrate this loading order for the valine precursor. Its mechanistic overlap with rxn_001 and rxn_002 is explicit; it is retained only as an alternative precursor-capture sequence.

reactions.name: Acid-promoted aminonitrile hydrolysis to valine
agents: Aqueous hydronium supplied by local volcanic acidity

conditions.other: Proposed pH 1-3 after aminonitrile accumulation; sustained aqueous residence in an acidic geothermal pool. Track nitrile and amide disappearance rather than assuming a fixed completion time. Ammonia represents the ammonium component at this pH; valine is also protonated.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-promoted nitrile hydration gives a transient amino amide, followed by amide hydrolysis to valine and the ammonia component. The net reaction consumes two waters per aminonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Miller (1957) showed that aminonitrile hydrolysis could account for amino-acid accumulation during approximately week-long discharge experiments. That supports the reaction class, not completion of this particular precursor at every proposed pH and temperature. The acid window is a design hypothesis requiring kinetic validation. Volcanic acidity supplies a chemically justified agent without adding an arbitrary mineral catalyst.

reactions.name: Alternative alkaline aminonitrile hydrolysis to valine

conditions.other: Proposed pH 10-11 in warm alkaline freshwater or moderately saline pool water. Alkalinity is a solution reagent reservoir, not an assigned mineral catalyst. Products are predominantly valinate and ammonia; neutral-parent formulas include eventual proton equilibration. Residence time and conversion must be measured.

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxide-promoted nitrile hydration and subsequent amide cleavage give valinate, represented by its neutral parent valine.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative operating-condition extension of the hydrolysis chemistry discussed by Miller (1957), not a separately validated valine experiment. Alkaline hydrolysis is chemically possible, but rates at this modest alkalinity may be low and aminonitrile decomposition may compete. This is an alternative processing condition, not an additional carbon-skeleton construction mechanism.

reactions.name: Hypothesized carbon-dioxide capture and hydantoin formation

conditions.other: Concentrated ammonium/bicarbonate water near pH 8.5. A 0.5 M total inorganic-carbon reservoir and weeks-long residence are reaction-class reference conditions, not a validated valine recipe. CO2 represents the reactive inorganic-carbon component, predominantly bicarbonate in the bulk solution.

reactions.mechanism: Aminonitrile carbamylation, cyclization and rearrangement are represented as a net conversion to 5-isopropylhydantoin. Inorganic carbon supplies the additional hydantoin carbonyl carbon.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative valine-specific extension of Bucherer-Bergs chemistry. Pulletikurti et al. (2022) support aminonitrile/hydantoin chemistry for other alpha-ketoacid systems, but the supplied research does not demonstrate this valine aminonitrile conversion. Hydantoin formation provides a chemically meaningful alternative to direct nitrile hydrolysis; its rate, selectivity and concentration requirements must be tested.

reactions.name: Hypothesized hydrolytic opening of isopropylhydantoin

conditions.other: Proposed pH approximately 8.5 in concentrated ammonium/bicarbonate solution. Use the 14-day warm phase of the reaction-class reference procedure as an initial observation window, not a guaranteed completion time. Maintain liquid water and monitor ring-opening regioselectivity.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of a hydantoin amide bond opens the ring to N-carbamoylvaline.
reactions.reasoning: Pulletikurti et al. (2022) support hydantoin-to-N-carbamoyl-amino-acid hydrolysis in their studied systems. Applying it to 5-isopropylhydantoin is speculative in the supplied evidence. Ammonia-source chemistry influences hydrolysis, so the published general temperature schedule cannot establish a valine-specific yield or rate. This is a potential kinetic bottleneck.

reactions.name: Hypothesized N-carbamoylvaline hydrolysis

conditions.other: Continue the warm aqueous phase and determine whether decarbamoylation occurs near pH 8.5. The literature's nominal 14-day warm phase is a reference for the overall processing stage, not an independently established duration for this step. CO2 and ammonia products equilibrate with bicarbonate and ammonium.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolytic cleavage of the carbamoyl substituent liberates valine; the removed carbamoyl group ultimately yields carbon dioxide and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative valine-specific extrapolation from the N-carbamoyl-amino-acid sequence supported by Pulletikurti et al. (2022). The net coproducts follow carbamoyl hydrolysis rather than an arbitrary closure of an unresolved product mixture. Nevertheless, decarbamoylation under the proposed mild conditions is not demonstrated for this substrate and may prevent the hydantoin branches from yielding appreciable free valine.

reactions.name: Hypothesized Bucherer-Bergs capture of alpha-ketoisovalerate

conditions.other: Reaction-class reference composition: 0.35 M ketoacid, 0.42 M total cyanide, 0.70 M total ammonium/ammonia and 0.5 M bicarbonate at pH 8.5, with an initial 21-day residence. These concentrations were not validated for alpha-ketoisovalerate. From a hypothetical 5 mM ketoacid source, reaching 0.35 M would require at least 70-fold concentration without loss; that source concentration is not established.

reactions.mechanism: A proposed aminonitrile/carbamate/cyclization sequence forms a carboxylated isopropylhydantoin while retaining the substrate carboxyl group temporarily.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative substrate extension of Pulletikurti et al. (2022), whose documented substrate set does not directly demonstrate alpha-ketoisovalerate-to-valine conversion. The carboxylated intermediate is a mechanistic hypothesis, not a reported valine-specific identification. The supplied branched ketoacid, concentrated cyanide/ammonia, long residence, and simultaneous solute retention are explicit bottlenecks. Evaporation alone does not establish their natural availability.

reactions.name: Hypothesized decarboxylation of carboxylated isopropylhydantoin

conditions.temperature: 300-353 K during the proposed staged processing
conditions.other: Monitor carbon dioxide release and hydantoin identity during the room-temperature and warm phases. No substrate-specific decarboxylation rate or preferred temperature is established.

reactions.mechanism: Loss of the substrate-derived carboxyl group followed by proton transfer produces 5-isopropylhydantoin. In this proposed atom mapping, cyanide subsequently supplies the valine carboxyl carbon.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative mechanistic resolution of the alpha-ketoacid Bucherer-Bergs reaction class described by Pulletikurti et al. (2022). It explicitly accounts for the carbon removed when the carboxylated intermediate becomes the ordinary hydantoin, but neither this intermediate nor its decarboxylation has been demonstrated for the valine substrate in the provided research. Isotope tracing is needed to test the proposed atom mapping.

reactions.name: Nickel-catalyzed reductive amination of alpha-ketoisovalerate
agents: Ni/SiO2-Al2O3 with accessible reduced nickel sites

conditions.other: Reported reference conditions: 30 mM alpha-ketoisovalerate, five equivalents NH4HCO3, pH 8, 72 h, and 10 mol% Ni relative to substrate. Use an oxygen-free, cyanide-free reactor. A natural analogue would require a confined H2-rich cool mineral interface; aged nickel sulfide is not assumed equivalent to the tested supported catalyst.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia forms an imine/iminium-type intermediate with the ketoacid; surface-activated hydrogen reduces it to valine.
reactions.reasoning: Direct valine experiment: Kaur et al. (2024). Their approximately 20% combined amino- and hydroxy-acid yield with a 34:66 ratio implies about 6.8% valine, an arithmetic inference rather than a separately reported yield. Catalyst-free controls did not reduce the substrate. Nickel offers a geochemically motivated active metal, but the engineered support, metal surface state, passivation and supplied 30 mM branched ketoacid prevent this from establishing a natural end-to-end synthesis.

reactions.name: Palladium-catalyzed reductive amination benchmark

conditions.other: Reported reference conditions: 30 mM alpha-ketoisovalerate, five equivalents NH4HCO3, pH 8, 72 h, and 1 mol% Pd relative to substrate. Oxygen and cyanide are excluded. This is a laboratory mineral-interface comparator; naturally available Pd/C is not assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Palladium activates hydrogen and promotes hydrogenation of the ketoacid-derived imine or iminium species.
reactions.reasoning: Direct valine experiment: Kaur et al. (2024). Approximately 77% combined yield and an 83:17 amino:hydroxy ratio imply about 64% valine. This provides the strongest reported selectivity among the three catalysts, but palladium scarcity and the engineered carbon-supported catalyst substantially weaken its prebiotic environmental case. It is retained for its experimentally demonstrated chemistry, not promoted as a demonstrated terrestrial source.

reactions.name: Meteoritic-metal reductive amination of alpha-ketoisovalerate
agents: Ground Aletai iron meteorite containing nickel-bearing metal

conditions.other: Reported reference conditions: 30 mM alpha-ketoisovalerate, five equivalents NH4HCO3, pH 8, 72 h, and 3 mg ground meteorite per experimental vial. The supplied report does not specify enough reactor-volume or exposed-metal-area information to scale that loading environmentally. Freshly exposed metal, anoxia and exclusion of cyanide are required assumptions.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrogen activation on reactive meteoritic metal sites enables reduction of an ammonia-derived imine/iminium intermediate.
reactions.reasoning: Direct valine experiment: Kaur et al. (2024). Approximately 74% combined yield and an 18:82 amino:hydroxy ratio imply about 13% valine. Meteoritic metal has a clearer natural provenance than engineered Pd/C, but grinding, accessible nickel sites, corrosion and sulfide passivation matter. The exact catalytic site is not established, and the branched ketoacid remains an imported precursor.

reactions.name: Competing nickel-catalyzed ketoacid hydrogenation
agents: Ni/SiO2-Al2O3 with accessible reduced nickel sites

conditions.other: Same reaction mixture as rxn_012: 30 mM ketoacid, five equivalents NH4HCO3, pH 8, 72 h and 10 mol% Ni. This flux competes with rxn_012; it is not a later step in that pathway.

reactions.mechanism: Direct hydrogenation of the keto carbonyl gives 2-hydroxyisovaleric acid instead of valine.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) directly observed the competing hydroxy acid. The reported combined yield and product ratio imply approximately 13.2% hydroxy-acid yield. Including this branch prevents nickel-mediated substrate reduction from being equated with valine synthesis. This molecule is a terminal competing product in the present graph, despite using the schema's intermediate role.

reactions.name: Competing palladium-catalyzed ketoacid hydrogenation

conditions.other: Same reaction mixture as rxn_013: 30 mM ketoacid, five equivalents NH4HCO3, pH 8, 72 h and 1 mol% Pd. This is a competing flux, not part of the productive reaction sequence.

reactions.mechanism: Palladium-catalyzed carbonyl hydrogenation produces the alpha-hydroxy acid.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) reported a 17% hydroxy-acid share within the approximately 77% combined product yield, implying about 13.1% hydroxy-acid yield. Palladium favors valine more strongly than the other tested catalysts but does not eliminate this sink. Natural catalyst availability remains a separate limitation.

reactions.name: Competing meteoritic-metal ketoacid hydrogenation
agents: Ground Aletai iron meteorite containing nickel-bearing metal

conditions.other: Same reaction mixture as rxn_014: 30 mM ketoacid, five equivalents NH4HCO3, pH 8, 72 h and 3 mg ground meteorite per reference vial. Environmental scaling and metal-surface aging are unresolved.

reactions.mechanism: Surface-mediated hydrogenation of the keto carbonyl produces 2-hydroxyisovaleric acid.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) reported an 82% hydroxy-acid share within the approximately 74% combined yield, implying about 60.7% hydroxy-acid yield. This dominant competing flux is essential to evaluating the meteorite route: high total reduction does not imply high valine selectivity. No return pathway from this sink is assumed.

pathways.name: Imine-first Strecker synthesis with acidic hydrolysis
pathways.description: Supplied isobutyraldehyde enters the imine/aminonitrile sequence, followed by acidic aqueous hydrolysis. This is a literature-supported reaction family with proposed, rather than experimentally established, valine-specific pool conditions. The branched aldehyde source remains outside the demonstrated network.

pathways.name: Imine-first Strecker synthesis with alkaline hydrolysis
pathways.description: The same carbon-skeleton construction as P1 is followed by an alternative alkaline processing stage. This is a condition-resolved graph pathway, not an independent synthesis mechanism. Slow hydrolysis and aminonitrile decomposition are unresolved risks.

pathways.name: Cyanohydrin-first capture with acidic hydrolysis
pathways.description: A proposed cyanohydrin capture stage precedes ammonia enrichment and aminonitrile formation. Acidic hydrolysis then yields valine. The cyanohydrin loading order is not directly validated for prebiotic valine and may converge mechanistically on the ordinary imine sequence.

pathways.name: Cyanohydrin-first capture with alkaline hydrolysis
pathways.description: Combines the proposed cyanohydrin-first loading sequence with alkaline aminonitrile hydrolysis. It is a distinct operational sequence but carries both the untested precursor-capture assumption and the alkaline-hydrolysis kinetic uncertainty.

pathways.name: Imine-first synthesis through a hydantoin reservoir
pathways.description: The aldehyde-derived aminonitrile is diverted into a hypothesized isopropylhydantoin, then hydrolyzed through N-carbamoylvaline. The valine-specific cyclization and final hydrolysis are not established by the supplied literature. Concentrated inorganic carbon and prolonged aqueous processing are required hypotheses.

pathways.name: Cyanohydrin-first synthesis through a hydantoin reservoir
pathways.description: The alternative cyanohydrin loading sequence feeds the same hypothesized hydantoin and N-carbamoyl intermediates as P5. This is a distinct graph path assembled from explicitly conditional steps, not an additional direct experimental demonstration.

pathways.name: Alpha-ketoisovalerate Bucherer-Bergs hypothesis
pathways.description: Supplied alpha-ketoisovalerate undergoes proposed cyanide/ammonia/inorganic-carbon capture, decarboxylation and hydantoin hydrolysis. Pulletikurti et al. (2022) support the reaction class, not this substrate-specific route. Concentration, atom mapping, decarboxylation and decarbamoylation all require validation.

pathways.name: Supported-nickel hydrogen reductive amination
pathways.description: Directly demonstrated conversion of supplied alpha-ketoisovalerate to valine under the Kaur et al. conditions. The approximate inferred valine yield is 6.8%. Hydroxy-acid formation competes through rxn_015 and is not included as a productive step. Natural precursor concentration and catalyst equivalence remain unresolved.

pathways.name: Palladium hydrogen reductive-amination benchmark
pathways.description: Directly demonstrated, comparatively selective conversion of supplied alpha-ketoisovalerate, with an approximate inferred valine yield of 64%. This is a laboratory-supported catalytic variant, not a demonstrated naturally available prebiotic system. The competing hydroxy-acid branch is rxn_016.

pathways.name: Meteoritic-metal hydrogen reductive amination
pathways.description: Directly demonstrated conversion over ground Aletai meteorite, with an approximate inferred valine yield of 13%. The catalyst has a natural provenance, but accessible metal area, corrosion and precursor supply are unresolved. Most measured reduction product is hydroxy acid through rxn_017, not valine.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a chemically coherent Strecker route from explicitly supplied isobutyraldehyde. Miller (1957) supports the general mechanism, while Ring et al. (1972) provide direct valine-product evidence from discharge chemistry, not validation of this exact surface-processing schedule. Reversible imine formation followed by cyanide trapping is reasonable. The principal unresolved implementation issue is the acidity, temperature and residence time required for aminonitrile hydrolysis. rxn_005 requires two waters, as established by the deterministic check, and has no conservation violation.
suggestions: Specify concentrations, pH, temperature and residence time for precursor capture and acidic hydrolysis, including how the solution changes between these stages.
Add reaction-level literature citations and valine-aminonitrile hydrolysis data under the proposed sheltered surface conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The carbon skeleton and Strecker capture chemistry are sound. Alkaline aminonitrile hydrolysis is chemically plausible, but the supplied research does not establish a valine-specific alkaline protocol for this setting. Its rate and selectivity depend on conditions that are not supplied in the reaction node. A basic environment alone does not establish useful conversion on the available timescale. rxn_006 is balanced with two waters; the uncertainty is kinetic and environmental, not stoichiometric.
suggestions: Provide an experimentally supported alkaline hydrolysis temperature, pH and duration for this aminonitrile.
Explain how alkaline processing follows precursor capture and quantify conversion relative to intermediate loss or incomplete hydrolysis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Cyanohydrin formation is credible, and the network correctly presents it as an alternative capture sequence rather than an independent amination mechanism. rxn_004 is plausible as a net conversion through reversible carbonyl release and subsequent imine/aminonitrile chemistry; it should not imply established direct displacement of hydroxyl by ammonia. Productive release from the cyanohydrin reservoir and the acidic hydrolysis schedule remain insufficiently characterized for the stated environment.
suggestions: Document cyanohydrin-to-aminonitrile conversion kinetics and speciation at the proposed ammonia concentration and pH.
Specify the acidic hydrolysis stage and demonstrate that cyanohydrin storage does not predominantly cause sequestration or precursor loss.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This sequence is atom-conserving and chemically possible, but combines two implementation uncertainties: productive conversion of the cyanohydrin pool and valine-specific alkaline nitrile hydrolysis. Neither is resolved by the broad Surface designation. The alternative-reactor framing avoids an assumed incompatibility with the metal-catalyzed branches, but does not specify the conditions within this pathway.
suggestions: Establish a staged cyanohydrin-capture, ammoniation and alkaline-hydrolysis protocol with measured intermediate and valine recoveries.
Provide quantitative pH, temperature, concentration and residence-time requirements rather than relying on the environment label.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The hydantoin and N-carbamoylvaline formulas are consistent with the proposed transformations, and all steps conserve atoms. General Bucherer-Bergs chemistry supports this reaction family. Pulletikurti et al. (2022) provide related hydantoin/carbamoyl precedent, but not direct validation of this aldehyde-derived valine sequence. Hydantoin storage is a plausible hypothesis; subsequent release of free valine requires demonstrated ring-opening and decarbamoylation rates. Correct hypothesis labeling improves literature alignment but does not establish those rates.
suggestions: Demonstrate formation and structural identity of 5-isopropylhydantoin from the valine aminonitrile under a specified CO2/bicarbonate regime.
Measure sequential hydantoin opening and N-carbamoylvaline hydrolysis under the proposed thermal and pH schedule, including intermediate persistence and decomposition.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a coherent hypothetical route if the cyanohydrin pool supplies aminonitrile and the hydantoin reservoir subsequently releases valine. It shares the hydantoin uncertainties of P5 and adds an unresolved precursor-release step. The network appropriately avoids claiming an independent elementary amination mechanism. Nevertheless, related reaction-class evidence does not demonstrate the complete valine-specific sequence or establish that the proposed reservoirs are productive rather than persistent sinks.
suggestions: Quantify carbon partitioning among cyanohydrin, aminonitrile, hydantoin, N-carbamoylvaline and free valine.
Establish compatible staged conditions for precursor release, CO2 capture and hydrolysis, with explicit concentration and residence mechanisms.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway is balanced and has relevant alpha-ketoacid Bucherer-Bergs precedent, but remains the least established productive sequence. Pulletikurti et al. (2022) did not directly test alpha-ketoisovalerate. The specific identity of mol_014 and its decarboxylation at the assigned stage require validation; formula balance alone does not establish either. The concentrated, weeks-long formation and heated hydrolysis conditions in the analogous research also need a concrete implementation in the stated surface setting.
suggestions: Provide a structural identifier for the proposed 5-carboxy-5-isopropylhydantoin and directly test its formation and decarboxylation.
Use carbon labeling to establish the fate of the original ketoacid carboxyl carbon, cyanide carbon and bicarbonate carbon.
Specify and justify substrate/buffer concentrations, the room-temperature residence period and subsequent heated hydrolysis instead of assuming transferability of the published protocol.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kaur et al. (2024) directly demonstrated this precursor-to-valine conversion over supported nickel. rxn_015 is also experimentally supported and is scored here as competing chemistry, not as a second productive step. The reported 20% combined product yield and 34:66 amino:hydroxy ratio imply approximately 6.8% valine yield, not 20%. The main uncertainty is implementing the tested hydrogen pressure, active nickel/support preparation and solution composition in the stated environment. The supplied ketoacid is an explicit scope boundary, not a connectivity defect.
suggestions: Attach the tested conditions to rxn_012 and rxn_015: 30 mM ketoacid, five equivalents NH4HCO3, pH 8, 22 degrees C, 5 bar H2, 72 hours and 10 mol% Ni on SiO2-Al2O3.
Specify hydrogen confinement, catalyst surface state and physical exclusion of cyanide; use the measured valine/hydroxy-acid partition rather than stoichiometry as a yield estimate.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the strongest demonstrated conversion by productive yield and selectivity in the supplied evidence. Kaur et al. (2024) report 77% combined products with an 83:17 valine:hydroxy-acid ratio, implying approximately 64% valine yield. rxn_016 is a supported competing sink, not a productive pathway step. The benchmark designation is appropriate: experimentally effective Pd/C does not establish the natural availability of an equivalent catalyst. Its high ranking concerns demonstrated synthesis, not a preferred historical origin scenario.
suggestions: Record the complete Kaur protocol, including 1 mol% Pd as Pd/C, and preserve the distinction between combined product yield and inferred valine yield.
Identify Pd/C explicitly as a supplied benchmark catalyst; any proposed geochemical implementation needs separate evidence for catalyst availability, hydrogen containment and resistance to poisoning.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Kaur et al. (2024) directly demonstrated valine formation using ground Aletai meteorite. The 74% combined yield and 18:82 amino:hydroxy ratio imply approximately 13% valine yield, with hydroxy-acid formation dominating. rxn_017 is correctly represented as competing chemistry and is not an additional productive step. The tested material gives this route a concrete environmental analogue, but its activity cannot automatically be assigned to arbitrary Ni-bearing minerals. Accessible metal surfaces, hydrogen retention and catalyst passivation remain implementation questions.
suggestions: Record the complete reaction conditions and normalize the reported 3 mg meteorite loading to solution volume, composition and accessible surface area.
Test the effect of surface aging and realistic solution components while documenting cyanide exclusion and the physical source and confinement of H2.

evaluation.network_feedback: The 15-molecule, 17-reaction graph is connected, contains sufficient nodes and uses molecule IDs consistently. The deterministic check establishes conservation for every reaction; rxn_005 and rxn_006 require two waters and are not conservation violations. Supplied isobutyraldehyde and alpha-ketoisovalerate are legitimate starting materials: missing upstream synthesis limits the claimed scope but is not itself a validity defect. Literature alignment is strong in distinguishing demonstrated Kaur conversions, established Strecker reaction classes and untested valine-specific hydantoin hypotheses. Alternative processing variants are not counted as independent experimental support. The competing reactions rxn_015-rxn_017 are assessed alongside their corresponding productive reactions without being counted as productive steps. Remaining weaknesses are missing reaction-specific conditions and citations, unverified hydantoin/decarboxylation assignments, and incomplete physical specifications for concentration, staged hydrolysis, hydrogen confinement and active catalyst availability. Cyanide separation and UV shielding are sensible requirements but need concrete implementation. Unspecified target stereochemistry is compatible with racemic synthesis. P9 is the best demonstrated synthetic benchmark, not an established preferred geochemical route. The complete network remains below the 0.90 approval threshold despite containing individually strong pathways.
